L105: # Embarrassingly Simple Self-Distillation Improves Code Generation
L106: 
L107: Ruixiang Zhang^{∗}  Richard He Bai^{∗}  Huangjie Zheng^{∗}  Navdeep Jaitly  Ronan Collobert
L108: Yizhe Zhang^{∗} Affiliation: Apple

L111: August 24, 2026 ^{∗} Equal contribution
L112: ###### Abstract
L113: Can a large language model (LLM) improve at code generation using only its own raw outputs, without a verifier, a teacher model, or reinforcement learning? We answer in the affirmative with simple self-distillation (SSD): sample solutions from the model with certain temperature and truncation configurations, then fine-tune on those samples with standard supervised fine-tuning.
L114: SSD improves Qwen3-30B-Instruct from 42.4% to 55.3% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v6, with gains concentrating on harder problems, and it generalizes across Qwen and Llama models at 4B, 8B, and 30B scale, including both instruct and thinking variants.
L115: To understand why such a simple method can work, we trace these gains to a precision-exploration conflict in LLM decoding and show that SSD reshapes token distributions in a context-dependent way, suppressing distractor tails where precision matters while preserving useful diversity where exploration matters. Taken together, SSD offers a complementary post-training direction for improving LLM code generation.

Left: SSD samples from the base model with training-time decoding temperature $T_{\textsf{train}}$, fine-tunes on its own raw outputs, and then decodes at evaluation time with $T_{\textsf{eval}}$; it uses no RL, verifier, teacher, or code execution environment.

The footer highlights the broader pattern: all five evaluated models improve, Qwen3-30B-Instruct gains +30% relative pass@1, and the largest gains occur on harder problems.
L119: ## 1 Introduction
L120: As LLMs are deployed to increasingly difficult coding tasks, the supply of high-quality supervised signal has become a binding constraint: human-written solutions (【92†Chen et al., 2021】; 【93†Austin et al., 2021】; 【94†Hendrycks et al., 2021a】) are expensive to produce, and synthetic data pipelines require either a stronger teacher model (【95†Hinton et al., 2015】; 【96†Kim and Rush, 2016】; 【97†Hsieh et al., 2023】; 【98†Agarwal et al., 2024】) or execution-based verification for every training problem (【99†Li et al., 2022】; 【100†Le et al., 2022】; 【101†Singh et al., 2024】; 【102†Liu et al., 2025】).
L121: Teacher-based distillation also inherits the ceiling of the teacher, while reinforcement learning with verifiable reward remains operationally complex and can be unstable, even in recent RL-based reasoning and coding pipelines (【103†He et al., 2026】; 【104†Shao et al., 2024】; 【105†DeepSeek-AI, 2025】; 【106†OpenAI, 2025】).
L122: Unsupervised alternatives that use intrinsic rewards such as majority voting or entropy minimization (【107†Zuo et al., 2025】; 【108†Agarwal et al., 2025】) have shown early promise but face reward hacking and collapse under extended training (【109†Zhang et al., 2025】). This raises a natural question: can a model improve itself without leveraging any external labeled data or verification at all?
L123: We show the answer is yes. Our method, simple self-distillation (SSD), is embarrassingly simple: sample solutions from the base model with specified temperature and truncation, then fine-tune on those raw, unverified samples via standard cross-entropy loss. This method requires only a set of problem prompts and the model itself: no human-labeled solutions, no reference answers, no teacher model, no reward model, no verifier, no execution environment, and no reinforcement learning of any kind.
L124: Table 1: Comparison of training paradigms.
L125: Surprisingly, it works. SSD improves Qwen3-30B-Instruct from 42.4% to 55.3% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v6 (【110†Jain et al., 2024】), with especially large gains on hard problems. Coverage improvements are larger still: hard-problem pass@5 rises from 31.1% to 54.1%, suggesting that SSD preserves useful exploration across solution branches instead of only sharpening a single dominant mode.
L126: These gains are not model-specific: SSD generalizes across five models spanning two families, three scales, and both instruct and thinking models.
L127: We study why such a simple method can work in the domain of code generation, which serves as a particularly useful testbed because the task structure makes the underlying mechanism especially visible. Code interleaves fork positions, where several continuations are genuinely plausible and may correspond to different solution approaches, with lock positions, where syntax and semantics leave little ambiguity but a low-probability distractor tail still remains.
L128: These two context types make contradictory demands on decoding temperature $T_{\textsf{eval}}$. Lowering $T_{\textsf{eval}}$ secures locks but starves forks of diversity, while raising it enables exploration at forks but lets distractors flood back in at locks. The best global decoding setting is therefore necessarily a compromise; we call this tension the precision-exploration conflict.
L129: SSD can be understood through this lens. Training on temperature-shifted, truncated samples implicitly reshapes the model’s distributions in a context dependent way (we formalize this later as support compression and within support reshaping in Equation (【111†4】)): it suppresses distractors most aggressively at locks while preserving useful diversity at forks.
L130: Evidence from controlled simulation and real-model analysis (【18†Section 4.2】), together with theoretical analysis (【44†Appendix B】), supports this account and explains why changing only the decoding settings cannot recover the gains. More broadly, this suggests that existing code models contain capability not realized under fixed decoding alone.
L131: Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that SSD can substantially improve code generation models’ performance using only their own unverified outputs, without any external teacher, verifier, reward model, or labeled solutions. Second, we identify the precision-exploration conflict and argue that it is the key mechanism behind SSD. Third, we support this mechanism with aligned evidence from controlled simulation, real-model analysis, and theory.
L132: ## 2 Embarrassingly Simple Self-Distillation (SSD)
L133: #### Data synthesis.
L134: 
L135: We write $T$ for the temperature and $\rho$ for the truncation configuration, namely the top-$k$ and top-$p$ used in decoding (see 【38†Appendix A】 for the precise decoding procedure). Given a frozen pre-trained LLM $p_{\theta}$ and a set of prompts $\mathcal{X}$, we sample $N$ candidate solutions per problem:
L136: 
L137:  | $$y\sim\textsf{Decode}_{T_{\textsf{train}},\,\rho_{\textsf{train}}}\!\big[p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\big]$$  |  | (1)
L138: The solutions are not verified in any way: no execution, no test cases, no filtering by correctness. The raw outputs form the simple self-distillation dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{SSD}}$. In practice, $N{=}1$ (a single sample per prompt) already suffices (【11†Section 3】).
L139: #### Training.
L140: 
L141: We fine-tune the model on $\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{SSD}}$ with standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT):
L142: 
L143:  | $$\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\textsf{SSD}}}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})$$  |  | (2)
L144: #### Inference.
L145: 
L146: The fine-tuned model $p_{\theta^{*}}$ is deployed with evaluation-time decoding configuration $(T_{\textsf{eval}},\rho_{\textsf{eval}})$:
L147: 
L148:  | $$\hat{y}\sim\textsf{Decode}_{T_{\textsf{eval}},\,\rho_{\textsf{eval}}}\!\big[p_{\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid x)\big]$$  |  | (3)

L150: ## 3 Experiments
L151: ### 3.1 Experimental Setup
L152: Models. We evaluate SSD on five models spanning two families (Llama, Qwen), three scales (4B–30B), and two reasoning styles (instruct, thinking): Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (dense, 8B), Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (dense, 4B; hereafter Qwen3-4B-Instruct), Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 (dense, 4B; hereafter Qwen3-4B-Thinking), Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (MoE, 30B total / 3B active; hereafter Qwen3-30B-Instruct), and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (MoE, 30B / 3B active; hereafter Qwen3-30B-Thinking).
L153: We apply SSD to each of these base models.
L154: Data synthesis. We use the seed subset of the rSTARcoder dataset (【102†Liu et al., 2025】), de-duplicated to yield ${\sim}$10K unique competitive programming problems. For each prompt we sample a single solution from the base model using the per-model generation decoding configuration in 【112†Table 4】. We apply only minimal syntactic filtering to remove empty responses and single line stubs, meaning there is absolutely no correctness signal used.
L155: Generation uses vLLM (【113†Kwon et al., 2023】) with 128K maximum sequence length limit.
L156: Training. We fine-tune with Megatron-LM^{1}^{1} 1 【114†https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM†github.com】 on 8$\times$B200 GPUs (EP${=}$8 for MoE models), using AdamW with cosine decay (peak LR $5\times 10^{-6}$), global batch size 32, sequence length 65,536, and 2,500 iterations for instruct models and 300 iterations for thinking models. The learning rate is warmed-up with 250 and 50 iterations, respectively.
L157: Evaluation. Our primary benchmark is LiveCodeBench v6 (LCB v6; Feb--May 2025, following the version split adopted by recent model releases ^{2}^{2} 2 【115†https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507†huggingface.co】; stratified by easy/medium/hard). We report LCB v5 (Aug 2024–Feb 2025, following the version split adopted by rSTARcoder (【102†Liu et al., 2025】)) as a secondary confirmation. The primary metric is pass@1; we also report pass@5 and per-difficulty breakdowns.
L158: Base-model results use each model’s officially recommended sampling parameters (【112†Table 4】); SSD models are evaluated with the decoding settings in 【112†Table 4】. Full experimental details, prompt formatting, and decoding settings are given in 【82†Section C.1】.
L159: ### 3.2 SSD Improves Code Generation Across the Board
L160: 
L161: Table 2: SSD improves every evaluated model on LiveCodeBench, with the largest gains on medium and hard problems. Results on LCB v6 and LCB v5, broken down by difficulty and grouped by reasoning style (thinking vs. instruct). Within each model pair, the first row is the base model and the second is +SSD; cell shading encodes the change relative to the base row (green = improvement, red = decrease).【116†Image: [Uncaptioned image]】
L162: SSD yields large gains on LiveCodeBench. On LCB v6, SSD improves Qwen3-30B-Instruct from 42.4% to 55.3% pass@1 (+12.9pp, +30.4% relative). The gains are broad across the evaluated models: Llama-8B improves by +3.5pp, Qwen3-4B-Instruct by +7.5pp, Qwen3-4B-Thinking by +3.3pp, and Qwen3-30B-Thinking by +2.1pp. Substantial gains also appear on the larger 374-problem LCB v5, where Qwen3-30B-Instruct improves from 45.8% to 54.3% pass@1 (+8.5pp).
L163: For a recipe based only on self-generated, unverified solutions and standard supervised fine-tuning, these are consistently strong improvements.
L164: SSD helps most on harder problems. For Qwen3-30B-Instruct on LCB v6, pass@1 improves by +6.5pp on easy problems, +14.2pp on medium problems, and +15.3pp on hard problems. The same concentration appears at pass@5, where the gains are +6.6pp on easy, +19.6pp on medium, and +23.0pp on hard. A similar pattern is visible in the Qwen thinking models: for Qwen3-4B-Thinking, hard pass@1 improves by +4.1pp versus +1.3pp on easy problems, and for Qwen3-30B-Thinking, the corresponding gains are +5.2pp versus +0.2pp.
L165: Across 【117†Table 2】, the medium and hard splits consistently account for the largest absolute gains.
L166: SSD does not collapse diversity. A second clear pattern in the table is that the gains are often larger at pass@5 than at pass@1, indicating that SSD preserves and even improves generation diversity. Across the Qwen models on LCB v6, the pass@5 gain exceeds the corresponding pass@1 gain: +15.8pp versus +7.5pp for Qwen3-4B-Instruct, +3.9pp versus +3.3pp for Qwen3-4B-Thinking, +18.1pp versus +12.9pp for Qwen3-30B-Instruct, and +3.5pp versus +2.1pp for Qwen3-30B-Thinking.
L167: For Qwen3-30B-Instruct, the same asymmetry is even larger on the hard subset, where pass@5 rises by +23.0pp while pass@1 rises by +15.3pp; on LCB v5, pass@5 likewise improves more than pass@1 (+12.0pp versus +8.5pp). These larger pass@5 gains are consistent with improved diversity across generation samples.
L168: Because SSD is trained only on competitive-programming data, a natural concern is that it may hurt performance outside that domain. To test this, we evaluate the same trained model out of the box on benchmarks for math reasoning, general code generation, and code understanding, without any additional training or adaptation. Performance remains broadly stable for the 30B models, see 【84†Section C.3】.
L169: ### 3.3 Global Decoding Policies Cannot Match SSD
L170: Figure 2: SSD outperforms the best point in the evaluated base-model decoding sweep within standard global decoding policies. Each panel shows one model (30B-Instruct, 4B-Instruct, 4B-Thinking) and one metric (pass@1 or pass@5); amber curves sweep base-model evaluation temperature while blue horizontal lines mark SSD results from 【117†Table 2】. Solid shading marks the margin over all problems; outlined (dashed-border) shading marks the margin on hard problems.
L171: Could the gains in 【117†Table 2】 be recovered without training, by tuning only evaluation-time decoding on the original base model? We test this within the standard family of global temperature and truncation $(T_{\textsf{eval}},\rho_{\textsf{eval}})$ decoding policies, sweeping evaluation-time decoding settings on the base model and comparing the best evaluated base-model configuration to SSD.
L172: For this comparison, we follow the officially recommended sampling settings for each model (see 【112†Table 4】) and sweep temperature extensively to probe the strongest decode-only performance achievable by the base model. 【118†Figure 2】 visualizes representative temperature sweeps and the remaining gap to SSD.
L173: Temperature tuning yields only modest gains on the base model. The base-model sweep curves are strikingly flat: for Qwen3-30B-Instruct, pass@1 ranges from 41.3% to 43.5% across the evaluated temperatures, a spread of only 2.2 pp. The other models show similarly narrow ranges (1.5–3.0 pp; 【118†Figure 2】).
L174: SSD still outperforms the best-tuned base model, especially on hard problems and at pass@5. Comparing SSD against the best-tuned base model, pass@1 advantages remain: +11.8 pp for Qwen3-30B-Instruct, +5.8 pp for Qwen3-4B-Instruct, +2.2 pp for Qwen3-4B-Thinking, and +1.1 pp for Qwen3-30B-Thinking. The gap widens on hard problems: for Qwen3-30B-Instruct, SSD exceeds the best-tuned base model by +13.3 pp on hard pass@1 and +19.4 pp on hard pass@5, both larger than the corresponding all-problem margins.
L175: This pattern holds across all models, the SSD advantage is consistently largest on hard problems at pass@5. These persistent margins indicate that SSD produces changes in the model itself in ways no decoding configuration can replicate, an effect we investigate in 【16†Section 4】.
L176: ### 3.4 How SSD Hyperparameters Interact
L177: To understand the best configuration of training and inference hyperparameters for SSD, we performed a grid search over $T_{\textsf{train}}$, and evaluated each checkpoint at multiple $T_{\textsf{eval}}$, with Qwen3-30B-Instruct on LCB v6. We compare two regimes: a no-truncation ablation, where temperature composition is cleanest, and the full truncated setting, where training-time truncation provides an additional gain channel. Full details are in 【83†Section C.2】.
L178: 【119†Image: Refer to caption】 Figure 3: Training and evaluation temperatures compose through a broad effective-temperature band, while truncation raises the achievable pass@1 within that band. (a) Representative Qwen3-30B-Instruct sweeps on LCB v6 against $T_{\textsf{eff}}=T_{\textsf{train}}T_{\textsf{eval}}$: gray = no truncation, amber/green = truncated training-time sampling. Dots are runs, curves are quadratic fits, and the dashed line marks the 42.4% baseline.
L179: (b) Qwen3-4B-Thinking on LCB v6 with truncation, shown as best pass@1 across iterations over $(T_{\textsf{train}},T_{\textsf{eval}})$.
L180: Without truncation, effective temperature organizes performance. $T_{\textsf{train}}$ and $T_{\textsf{eval}}$ trade off each other: $T_{\textsf{train}}$ controls how strongly SSD reshapes the model distribution, while $T_{\textsf{eval}}$ controls how aggressively decoding exploits that reshaped distribution. Define $T_{\textsf{eff}}=T_{\textsf{train}}\cdot T_{\textsf{eval}}$; we show that $T_{\textsf{eff}}$ governs performance.
L181: To isolate this, we run a search with only temperature scaling ($T_{\textsf{train}}\in\{0.5,0.7,1.0,1.5,2.0\}$ and $T_{\textsf{eval}}\in[0.6,1.5]$; 【120†Figure 3a】,【121†Figure 10】), and no truncation $\rho_{\textsf{train}}$. In this regime, the two temperatures compose cleanly: configurations are well governed by $T_{\textsf{eff}}$, with $R^{2}{=}0.75$ and a quadratic peak near $T_{\textsf{eff}}\approx 1.2$, as formalized in 【56†Section B.3】.
L182: This also explains why higher $T_{\textsf{train}}$ makes the model more responsive to $T_{\textsf{eval}}$: stronger training-time reshaping creates more room for evaluation-time decoding to trade off precision against diversity. Intuitively, higher $T_{\textsf{eff}}$ is preferred to have more diverse generation as long as the generation is not broken.
L183: With truncation, the performance ceiling rises. When a nontrivial training-time truncation configuration $\rho_{\textsf{train}}$ is used during SSD data generation, the truncated runs (amber/green in 【120†Figure 3a】) remain above the baseline across a wider range of $T_{\textsf{eff}}$ than the no-truncation runs (gray), though the exact collapse onto $T_{\textsf{eff}}$ no longer holds.
L184: This is expected: training-time truncation adds a second improvement channel on top of temperature composition by suppressing low-probability tails during data synthesis. Among the truncated runs, the best observed setting uses $T_{\textsf{train}}{=}2.0$, $T_{\textsf{eval}}{=}1.1$, and training-time top-$k{=}10$, reaching 49.7% pass@1 (+7.3 pp), above all no-truncation results. As expected, the optimal $T_{\textsf{eff}}$ generally shifts towards a higher temperature with more stringent truncation.
L185: Similarly, the diagonal-band pattern appears for Qwen3-4B-Thinking (【120†Figure 3b】,【122†Figure 11】), confirming that the temperature-composition structure extends to thinking models.
L186: ## 4 Why SSD Works
L187: The gains above raise a natural question: what changes inside the model during simple self-distillation, and why can’t the same effect be achieved by simply adjusting how the original model decodes? Our hypothesis is that the answer lies in a structural conflict in generation. Some tokens demand precision, others demand exploration, and any fixed decoding configuration must compromise between them. SSD helps by reshaping token distributions in a way that alleviates this conflict.
L188: We validate this mechanism in three steps: a controlled toy simulation, real model analysis, and theoretical decomposition.
L189: Figure 4: A single evaluation temperature cannot satisfy both exploration at forks and precision at locks. L221: The entire training pipeline requires only standard supervised training infrastructure: no reward models, no value functions, no advantage estimation, and no multi-rollout sampling. L236: Following the inverse RL framework of 【98†Shenfeld et al. (2026)】, we show that CRISP implicitly maximizes a reward function that combines task performance with a conciseness preference.

L238: ###### Theorem 1 (Implicit reward).

L240: The CRISP objective (Eq. 【119†1】) is equivalent to maximizing the expected implicit reward:
L241: 
L242:  | $$r(y_{t},x)=\log\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid x,c,y_{<t})-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).$$  |  | (3)

L244: 
L245: Expanding the reverse KL:

L247:  | $\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\|\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,c,y_{<t})\big)$  | $\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid x,c,y_{<t})}\right]$  |  | (4)

L251: The implicit reward $r(y_{t},x)$ is positive when the concise teacher assigns higher probability to token $y_{t}$ than the student does, and negative otherwise. Within each $M$-step window, the teacher weights $\bar{\theta}$ are fixed, serving as an implicit trust region: the student can only move as far as the teacher’s concise distribution allows, preventing unbounded policy drift.

L255: A natural concern is whether compression degrades accuracy. The following theorem shows that accuracy loss is bounded by two interpretable quantities.
L256: ###### Proof sketch.
L257: Apply Pinsker’s inequality to convert the KL bound $\epsilon_{\mathrm{KL}}$ into a total variation bound $\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{KL}}/2}$ between student and teacher distributions. Total variation bounds the difference in probability of any event, in particular the correctness event $A(x)$, so the student’s accuracy is within $\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{KL}}/2}$ of the teacher’s. Combining with the teacher quality assumption $\epsilon_{T}$ via the triangle inequality yields the result. ∎
L258: The bound decomposes accuracy loss into two independent, interpretable terms: teacher quality ($\epsilon_{T}$) and distillation gap ($\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{KL}}/2}$). When the concise teacher is at least as accurate as the base model ($\epsilon_{T}\leq 0$), the bound becomes $\mathrm{Acc}(\pi_{\theta^{*}})\geq\mathrm{Acc}(\pi_{\bar{\theta}})+|\epsilon_{T}|-\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{KL}}/2}$, so accuracy is preserved, and improves whenever the teacher’s gain exceeds the distillation gap.

L262: A key design question for any compression method is how to allocate budget across problems of varying difficulty. We show that CRISP handles this automatically: the compression signal is provably stronger on easy problems.
L263: ###### Proof sketch.
L264: Decompose the normalized KL into essential and compressible token contributions: $S(x)=\rho(x)\cdot D_{\mathcal{E}}+(1-\rho(x))\cdot D_{\mathcal{C}}$, where $\rho(x)$ is the fraction of essential tokens, and $D_{\mathcal{E}},D_{\mathcal{C}}$ are the category-level KL divergences.

L78: ###### Abstract
L79: On-policy self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) learns new skills from demonstrations while reducing forgetting, but it always distils toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher. This fixes teacher influence at the full-teacher endpoint, providing no control over how much demonstration information should be transferred at each prediction state. We introduce Information-Proximal SDFT (iSDFT), which instead treats the teacher as a budgeted source of information.
L80: At each token, iSDFT selects the distribution closest to the current student that satisfies a prescribed teacher-information constraint, yielding a closed-form exponential target with a locally determined tilt. To control cumulative drift, we further anchor the student to its frozen base policy. Across four heterogeneous LLM backbones and two specialisation tasks, iSDFT improves vanilla SDFT in 7 of 8 model-task settings and matches it in the remaining one.
L81: It also provides tighter retention on the original SDFT benchmark suite, with 73% of evaluations remaining within 0.5 points of the base model versus 52% for the strongest baseline, while achieving the largest mean improvement on all ten additional mathematics, coding, and competition-mathematics benchmarks. These results show that controlling how much and when teacher information is introduced improves specialisation while preserving broader capability.

L83: ## 1 Introduction
L84: Continual learning asks whether a model can acquire new capabilities without erasing those it already possesses (【65†McCloskey and Cohen, 1989】; 【66†Bou-Ammar et al., 2014】; 【67†Bou-Ammar et al., 2015】; 【68†Kirkpatrick et al., 2017】; 【69†Parisi et al., 2019】).
L85: This is the classical stability–plasticity dilemma: adaptation must be sufficiently plastic to incorporate new information, yet sufficiently stable to preserve previously acquired behaviour (【70†Hadsell et al., 2020】; 【71†De Lange et al., 2021】; 【72†Wang et al., 2024】).
L86: The problem is increasingly important for large language models (LLMs), which are routinely adapted after pre-training to follow new instructions, use tools, solve specialised tasks, or acquire domain knowledge (【73†Wei et al., 2022】; 【74†Schick et al., 2023】; 【75†Zhang et al., 2026】). Demonstrations provide a natural interface for such adaptation by showing the model the desired behaviour directly.
L87: Yet learning from demonstrations is not simply a problem of imitation: the model must acquire the demonstrated behaviour to learn the new skill without unnecessarily perturbing capabilities that already work (【76†Luo et al., 2025】; 【77†Shenfeld et al., 2026】).
L88: The standard approach to demonstration-based adaptation is supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which treats each prompt–completion pair as a labelled trajectory and maximises the likelihood of the expert response. This is simple, but off-policy: training occurs on expert-generated histories, whereas deployment unfolds on histories generated by the model itself (【78†Song et al., 2023】; 【72†Wang et al., 2024】; 【79†Chen et al., 2026a】; 【80†Lu et al., 2026】; 【81†Chen et al., 2026b】).
L89: Self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) (【77†Shenfeld et al., 2026】) addresses this mismatch while retaining the demonstration-learning interface. The student generates its own trajectories, and a demonstration-conditioned teacher provides token-level supervision on those same on-policy prefixes.
L90: This makes SDFT a particularly attractive starting point for continual learning: it requires neither preference labels nor reinforcement-learning rewards, while substantially reducing the mismatch between training and deployment.
L91: However, SDFT resolves only one part of the problem. By training on student-generated prefixes, it controls where the demonstration signal is applied; it does not control how strongly the teacher should influence the student at those states. At every token, SDFT uses the full demonstration-conditioned teacher distribution as the target, corresponding to the maximum-teacher-influence endpoint of the local stability–plasticity trade-off.
L92: The student is therefore asked to match the complete teacher distribution regardless of how strongly the demonstration changes its current predictive behaviour. We instead treat the teacher as a source of information rather than the target itself. This leads to a different formulation: prescribe how much teacher information the target should contain, then choose, among all targets satisfying that requirement, the one closest to the current student.
L93: #### Contributions.
L94: We formalise this idea as Information-Proximal Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (iSDFT). At each student-generated prefix, iSDFT selects the distribution closest to the current student that satisfies a prescribed teacher-information requirement. The resulting target has a closed-form exponential path between student and teacher, but crucially its local tilt is not chosen directly: it is induced by the information constraint at each prediction state.
L95: This introduces a new information-constrained target-selection principle for adaptive distillation, obtained by KL I-projection onto a teacher-information constraint set rather than prescribed through a hand-chosen or scheduled interpolation coefficient (【82†Shing et al., 2025】; 【83†Xu et al., 2026】).
L96: While this information-proximal construction makes each target locally conservative, it does not by itself control cumulative drift over adaptation: the current student serves as a moving reference, so a sequence of small local changes can still move the model substantially away from its pretrained behaviour.
L97: We therefore introduce a separate KL anchor to a frozen base policy, explicitly decoupling local plasticity toward the demonstrated behaviour from long-horizon preservation of previously acquired capabilities. The resulting method is simple to implement: the information constraint determines a token-specific distillation target, while a small KL penalty provides a fixed reference to the model before adaptation.
L98: Across four heterogeneous LLM backbones and two demonstration-driven specialisation tasks, iSDFT consistently improves upon vanilla SDFT: it improves task acquisition in seven of eight model–task settings and matches it in the remaining one. Crucially, these gains do not come at the expense of broader capability.
L99: On the original SDFT retention suite, iSDFT produces the tightest concentration around the base model and keeps $73\%$ of evaluations within $0.5$ points of the pretrained checkpoint, compared with $52\%$ for the strongest baseline at that tolerance. We further extend evaluation to ten held-out mathematics, coding, and competition-math benchmarks motivated by recent concerns that privileged self-distillation can degrade reasoning.
L100: On this broader suite, iSDFT achieves the largest mean improvement over the base model on all ten benchmarks, with particularly large gains on MATH-500, AIME24, and AMC23.
L101: ## 2 On-Policy Self-Distillation
L102: This section reviews on-policy SDFT and gives an information-geometric interpretation of its teacher-matching objective. Let $x$ denote a task prompt and let $c$ denote an in-context demonstration of the desired behaviour. In demonstration-based adaptation, $c$ provides an example of how the task should be solved, but the student must eventually produce a completion without being conditioned on that demonstration at inference time.
L103: Given the prompt $x$, the student, $\pi_{\theta}(\cdot)$, generates a completion $y=[y_{1},\dots,y_{T}]$ autoregressively, such that each token $y_{t}$ is sampled as follows: $y_{t}\sim\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(v|x,y_{<t})$. For notational ease, we write $\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)=\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(v|x,y_{<t})$ for all $v\in\mathcal{V}$ with $\mathcal{V}$ denoting the vocabulary. Importantly, the prefix $y_{<t}$ is not an expert prefix. It is produced by the student itself.
L104: Thus, the state on which learning occurs is part of the student’s own rollout distribution. SDFT constructs a teacher distribution by evaluating the same model on the same student-generated prefix, but with the demonstration $c$ added to the context: $\mathcal{T}_{t}(v)=\pi_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}}(v|x,y_{<t},c)$. Here, $c$ denotes the in-context demonstration, and $\bar{\bm{\theta}}$ denotes the teacher parameters.
L105: Depending on the implementation, these parameters may be tied to the student, treated as a stop-gradient copy (【84†Hübotter et al., 2026】), or maintained as an exponential moving average of the student parameters, as in (【77†Shenfeld et al., 2026】).
L106: Thus, the student and teacher differ through the information available at prediction time. The student predicts from the prompt and its own prefix, while the teacher predicts from the same prefix augmented with the demonstration. This is the key on-policy structure: the trajectory is generated by the student, but the target distribution is shaped by the demonstrated behaviour.
L107: Vanilla SDFT uses the context-conditioned distribution as the token-level target. The objective in the original SDFT can be written as:

L110: #### Information-Geometric Interpretation of SDFT for Continual Learning.
L111: The objective in Equation 【85†1】 has a simple local interpretation. For a fixed student-generated prefix $y_{<t}$, SDFT compares the student distribution $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ to the full context-conditioned teacher distribution $\mathcal{T}_{t}$.
L112: If we ignored parameterisation and optimised directly over the categorical distribution at this prefix, then: $\arg\min_{\mathcal{Q}\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\text{KL}(\mathcal{T}_{t}||\mathcal{Q})=\mathcal{T}_{t}.$ Thus, the local solution preferred by SDFT is the teacher itself. L113: This gives an information-geometric view of vanilla SDFT. At each on-policy state $y_{<t}$, the student distribution is pushed towards the context-conditioned teacher by minimising its KL divergence to $\mathcal{T}_{t}$. Consequently, SDFT corresponds to the full-influence endpoint of self-distillation: the teacher is not merely used to indicate a direction of improvement, but is treated as the complete local solution. In the language of continual learning, this corresponds to a maximum-plasticity choice.
L114: The update is allowed to move as far as needed towards the demonstrated behaviour, with no explicit constraint on how close the resulting target remains to the current student distribution.
L115: Our observation motivates the generalisation in the coming section. Rather than asking the student to move all the way towards $\mathcal{T}_{t}$, we introduce an intermediate target $\mathcal{Q}_{t}$ whose teacher influence is controlled. The target contains a prescribed amount of information from the teacher, but among all such distributions it should remain as close as possible to the current student.
L116: Vanilla SDFT is recovered when the prescribed information level equals the teacher’s own information level, i.e., when $\mathcal{Q}_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{t}$.
L117: ## 3 Info-Proximal Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning
L118: ### 3.1 Teacher Information and Local Plasticity
L119: At a fixed student-generated prefix $y_{<t}$, the two distributions $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{t}$ describe two different behaviours. The student distribution $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ represents the model’s current behaviour without access to the demonstration, while the teacher distribution $\mathcal{T}_{t}$ represents the behaviour induced by conditioning on the demonstration.
L120: To control the teacher’s influence, we first need a local measure of how the teacher changes the student’s predictive distribution. We define:
L121:  | $$\eta_{t}(v)=\log\frac{\mathcal{T}_{t}(v)}{\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)},\ \ \forall v\in\mathcal{V}.$$  |  | (2)
L122: This quantity is positive for tokens that the demonstration-conditioned teacher favours more than the current student, and negative for tokens that the student favours more than the teacher. Thus, $\eta_{t}(v)$ describes the local direction in which the demonstration changes the model’s next-token distribution.
L123: For any candidate target distribution $\mathcal{Q}_{t}(v)$, its teacher’s information-level is further defined as: $\mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q}_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\mathcal{Q}_{t}}[\eta_{t}(v)].$ A target with larger $\mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q}_{t})$ places more probability mass on tokens favoured by the demonstration-conditioned teacher. In this sense, $\mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q}_{t})$ measures local plasticity towards the demonstrated behaviour.
L124: Conversely, keeping $\mathcal{Q}_{t}$ close to $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ preserves the current student behaviour and corresponds to local stability.
L125: Rather than requiring the student to imitate the full teacher distribution, we seek a target that contains a prescribed amount of teacher-provided information while remaining as close as possible to the student’s current behaviour. This gives the information-proximal projection:
L126: 
L127:  | $$\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{Q}\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\text{KL}(\mathcal{Q}||\mathcal{P}_{t})\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q})\geq\gamma_{t},$$  |  | (3)
L128: with $\gamma_{t}$ being the local teacher-information budget. The objective favours stability by keeping the target close to the current student, while the constraint enforces plasticity by requiring the target to retain sufficient information from the demonstration-conditioned teacher.
L129: #### Information-Geometric View.
L130: The above constrained projection admits a natural interpretation from information geometry. To make this explicit, define the teacher-information feasible set $\mathcal{C}_{t}(\gamma_{t})=\{\mathcal{Q}\in\Delta(\mathcal{V}):\mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q})\geq\gamma_{t}\}$.
L131: The problem in Equation 【86†3】 can be rewritten as: $\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}=\Pi^{I}_{\mathcal{C}_{t}(\gamma_{t})}(\mathcal{P}_{t}):=\arg\min_{Q\in\mathcal{C}_{t}(\gamma_{t})}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|\mathcal{P}_{t}).$ In other words, Equation 【86†3】 can be re-interpreted as the KL $I$-projection of the current student distribution onto the teacher-information constraint set.
L132: When the constraint is active, the optimum lies on the boundary $\mathcal{I}_{t}(Q)=\gamma_{t}$: the information budget selects the admissible teacher-information level, while the $I$-projection chooses the minimum-KL displacement from the student. This view leads directly to the exponential target, as shown in Equation 【87†4】.
L133: This local notion of stability, however, is not sufficient for continual learning. The information-proximal projection limits how far the target moves from the current student at a particular prediction state.
L134: Continual learning, in contrast, requires new capabilities to be acquired without excessive degradation of previously learned behaviour, a central manifestation of the stability–plasticity dilemma and catastrophic forgetting (【65†McCloskey and Cohen, 1989】; 【68†Kirkpatrick et al., 2017】; 【66†Bou-Ammar et al., 2014】; 【70†Hadsell et al., 2020】).
L135: Crucially, our projection is defined relative to the current student, whereas preserving prior capabilities requires accounting for changes accumulated across adaptation. Since the student itself changes after every optimisation update, a sequence of locally conservative updates may still lead to substantial drift from its initial behaviour.
L136: To make this distinction explicit, consider the sequence of model distributions induced over optimisation, $\mathcal{P}^{(0)},\dots,\mathcal{P}^{(N)}$ where $n\in[1:N]$ indexes successive parameter updates. Even if every update is locally conservative, such that: $\text{KL}(\mathcal{P}^{(n+1)}||\mathcal{P}^{(n)})\leq\epsilon$ for all $n$, this does not imply that $\text{KL}(\mathcal{P}^{(N)}||\mathcal{P}^{(0)})$ is small.
L137: Thus, controlling each update relative to the current student does not, by itself, control the cumulative departure from the model before adaptation. We therefore retain a frozen copy of the initial student as a fixed behavioural reference. Let $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{base}}$ denote the next-token distribution of this frozen model, evaluated at the same prediction state as the current student. We then augment the information-proximal distillation objective with a base-policy anchoring term:
L138:  | $$\mathcal{\ell}_{t}=\text{KL}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}||\mathcal{P}_{t})+\mu\text{KL}(\mathcal{P}_{\text{base}}||\mathcal{P}_{t}),\ \ \text{with}\ \ \mu\geq 0\ \ \implies\ \ \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\left[\sum_{t}\ell_{t}\right].$$  |
L139: #### Characterising Local Plasticity.
L140: To better understand the structure of $\ell_{t}$, we next characterise the information-proximal target $\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}$. While the base-policy term has a direct interpretation as a fixed anchor to the model before adaptation, $\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}$ is defined only implicitly through the constrained projection in Equation 【86†3】. We therefore derive its closed-form solution and show how the teacher-information budget $\gamma_{t}$ determines the amount of local teacher influence.
L141: ###### Proposition 1 (Information-Proximal Target).
L142: 
L143: Assume that $\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)>0$ and $\mathcal{T}_{t}(v)>0$ for all $v\in\mathcal{V}$. Consider the information-proximal projection in Equation 【86†3】. When information constraint is active, then the optimal target is:
L144:  | $$\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}(v)=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)\exp\!\left(\lambda_{t}\eta_{t}(v)\right)}{\mathcal{Z}_{t}(\lambda_{t})},\ \ \mathrm{with}\ \ \mathcal{Z}_{t}(\lambda_{t})=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\mathcal{P}_{t}(u)\exp\!\left(\lambda_{t}\eta_{t}(u)\right).$$  |
L145: Here, $\mathcal{Z}_{t}(\lambda_{t})$ is the normalising constant, and $\lambda_{t}\geq 0$ is the Lagrange multiplier associated with the information constraint, chosen such that $\mathcal{I}_{t}(\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star})=\gamma_{t}.$ Equivalently, substituting $\eta_{t}(v)=\log\!\left(\mathcal{T}_{t}(v)/\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)\right)$ gives:
L146:  | $$\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}(v)=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)^{1-\lambda_{t}}\mathcal{T}_{t}(v)^{\lambda_{t}}}{\displaystyle\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\mathcal{P}_{t}(u)^{1-\lambda_{t}}\mathcal{T}_{t}(u)^{\lambda_{t}}}.$$  |  | (4)
L147: Proposition 【88†1】 characterises local plasticity through an exponential path between the current student $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ and the demonstration-conditioned teacher $\mathcal{T}_{t}$. Crucially, $\lambda_{t}$ is not a tuned interpolation weight, but the local Lagrange multiplier induced by the information budget $\gamma_{t}$. Thus, $\gamma_{t}$ specifies the required teacher information, while $\lambda_{t}$ determines the local tilt needed to realise it.
L148: ### 3.2 From Information Budget to Local Teacher Influence
L149: The expression in Equation 【87†4】 introduces a local tilt parameter $\lambda_{t}$, which controls how strongly the current student distribution is shifted toward the demonstration-conditioned teacher. This raises a natural question: how should $\lambda_{t}$ be chosen? A straightforward approach would be to treat it as an additional interpolation hyperparameter.
L150: However, a fixed interpolation strength has no consistent information-theoretic meaning across prediction states: when the student and teacher already agree, a given value of $\lambda_{t}$ may induce only a small change, whereas the same value can produce a much larger shift when their distributions differ substantially. Treating $\lambda_{t}$ as a free hyperparameter would therefore make the amount of transferred teacher information state-dependent in an uncontrolled way.
L151: Instead, we determine $\lambda_{t}$ from the teacher-information budget $\gamma_{t}$ itself. For each token position, we choose the value of $\lambda_{t}$ required for the resulting target $\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\star}$ to attain the prescribed information level.
L152: To determine this local tilt, consider the information level attained by the target as a function of $\lambda$. For any candidate $\lambda\geq 0$, let:
L153: 
L154:  | $$\mathcal{Q}_{t}(v;\lambda)=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{t}(v)\exp(\lambda\eta_{t}(v))}{\mathcal{Z}_{t}(\lambda)},\ \ \text{and}\ \ \mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda)=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\mathcal{Q}_{t}(\cdot;\lambda)}[\eta_{t}(v)].$$  |
L155: The desired $\lambda_{t}$ is therefore the solution of $\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda_{t})=\gamma_{t}$. The remaining question is whether the information constraint admits a well-defined local tilt. In particular, for a prescribed feasible budget $\gamma_{t}$, we would like to know whether there exists a value $\lambda_{t}$ such that $\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda_{t})=\gamma_{t}$ and whether this value is unique.
L156: To establish this, we characterise how the attained information level $\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda)$ varies with $\lambda$. Differentiating gives us:
L157:  | $$\frac{d}{d\lambda}\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda)=\mathrm{Var}_{v\sim\mathcal{Q}(\cdot;\lambda)}[\eta_{t}(v)]\geq 0\implies\ \mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda)\ \text{monotone non-decreasing in $\lambda$.}$$  |
L158: Consequently, for any $\gamma_{t}$ lying in the attainable range of $\mathcal{G}_{t}$, a solution $\lambda_{t}$ exists; moreover, whenever $\mathcal{G}_{t}$ is strictly increasing over the relevant interval, that solution is unique. Interestingly, this gives us a simple and practical procedure for computing $\lambda_{t}$. Rather than treating it as an independently tuned hyperparameter, we solve the scalar equation: $\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda_{t})=\gamma_{t}$ using one-dimensional root finding.
L159: In our implementation, we use bisection: if $\mathcal{G}_{t}(\lambda)<\gamma_{t}$, the tilt is increased; otherwise, it is decreased. Hence, once the desired information budget $\gamma_{t}$ is specified, the corresponding local teacher influence is determined automatically from the geometry of $\mathcal{P}_{t}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{t}$.
